# Marketing Strategy and Services {#marketing-strategy}

In the early 1990s many large manufacturers still described themselves by what
came off their assembly lines. Thirty years later, aircraft-engine makers sell
"hours of thrust", software firms sell subscriptions rather than licences, and
retailers compete on what they know about each customer as much as on what they
stock. Why do some firms sense these shifts early and others late? Why does a
bank with modern branches and competitive rates still lose customers to a rival
that simply answers the phone? Why is a subscriber who stays one extra year worth
so much more than a few points of price? And why do so many advertising plans
still assume that consumers move neatly from awareness to purchase?

These questions belong to **marketing strategy**: the set of theories that
explain how firms understand markets, create and deliver value, and allocate
marketing resources over time. This chapter covers seven of the field's most
influential frameworks. **[Market orientation](#market-orientation)** explains how organizations
generate and act on market intelligence. **[Service-dominant logic](#service-dominant-logic)** reframes
what is exchanged in markets. The **[gaps model of service quality](#service-quality-gap-model)** diagnoses
where service failures originate. **[Customer equity](#customer-equity)** treats customers as
financial assets. The **[hierarchy of effects](#hierarchy-of-effects)** models how advertising is
supposed to work. The **[product life cycle](#product-life-cycle)** describes how markets evolve, and
the **[marketing mix](#marketing-mix)** organizes the decisions a manager controls. Each is widely
taught and widely used, and each has attracted serious criticism. Understanding
both the logic and the critique is what separates a theory-informed strategist
from a framework user.

The seven frameworks fall into three groups. Market orientation and
service-dominant logic are theories of how a firm should *understand* markets and
value. The gaps model and customer equity are theories of how service and
customer relationships translate into *outcomes*, perceived quality in one case
and financial value in the other. The hierarchy of effects, the product life
cycle, and the marketing mix are planning frameworks for *managing* programs over
consumers' decision processes, over a market's evolution, and across the
decisions a manager controls. The first group draws on the
[resource-based](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)) and learning traditions. The second
draws on psychology and finance. The third is closest to everyday practice, and
for that reason it is the most in need of the critical scrutiny that later
research has supplied (Table \@ref(tab:tab-ms-glance)).

## Market Orientation {#market-orientation}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Businesses that systematically generate intelligence about
customers and competitors, share it across functions, and respond to it achieve
superior performance.

**Origins.** Marketing strategy. Two parallel 1990 articles in the *Journal of
Marketing*: a behavioural conceptualization by @kohli1990 and a cultural one by
@narver1990. Meta-analysed by @kirca2005.

**Level of analysis.** Strategic business unit or firm.

**Key constructs.** Intelligence generation, intelligence dissemination,
responsiveness, customer orientation, competitor orientation, interfunctional
coordination, market turbulence, competitive intensity.

**Boundary conditions.** Benefits depend on whether customer needs are knowable
and changing, on the cost of collecting intelligence, and on whether responding
to current customers diverts resources from disruptive opportunities.

**Related theories.** [Resource-based theory](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)),
[Market-based assets](#market-based-assets) (Section \@ref(market-based-assets)),
[Dynamic capabilities](#dynamic-capabilities-framework) (Section \@ref(dynamic-capabilities-framework)),
[Absorptive capacity](#absorptive-capacity) (Section \@ref(absorptive-capacity)),
[Organizational learning](#organizational-learning) (Section \@ref(organizational-learning)),
[Disruptive innovation](#disruptive-innovation) (Section \@ref(disruptive-innovation)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

The **marketing concept**, the idea that a business should be organized around
satisfying customer needs profitably, had been a staple of textbooks since the
1950s. What it lacked was a definition precise enough to measure. In 1990 two
research teams independently supplied one. @kohli1990 reviewed the literature
and interviewed managers across functions and industries. They defined **market
orientation** as the organization-wide *generation* of market intelligence about
current and future customer needs, the *dissemination* of that intelligence
across departments, and organization-wide *responsiveness* to it. Their
definition is behavioural: market orientation is something a business *does*.

@narver1990 took a cultural view. Market orientation, in their account, is the
[organizational culture](#organizational-culture) (Section \@ref(organizational-culture)) that most effectively creates the behaviours needed to
deliver superior value to buyers. It has three behavioural components, **customer
orientation**, **competitor orientation**, and **interfunctional coordination**,
and two decision criteria, a long-term focus and profitability. Using data from
140 strategic business units of a single corporation, they reported a
substantial positive association between market orientation and profitability.

The two conceptualizations were soon operationalized in widely used scales:
MARKOR for the behavioural view [@kohli1993] and the Narver and Slater scale for
the cultural view. @day1994 then reframed the construct as a set of
**capabilities**, notably *market sensing* and *customer linking*, connecting
market orientation to the [resource-based view](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)) and
to later work on [market-based assets](#market-based-assets) (Section \@ref(market-based-assets))
[@srivastava1998] (Table \@ref(tab:tab-ms-mo-views)).

```{r tab-ms-mo-views}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Feature, ~`Behavioural view`, ~`Cultural view`,
  "Key source", "Kohli & Jaworski (1990)", "Narver & Slater (1990)",
  "Definition", "Generation, dissemination, and use of market intelligence", "Culture that creates behaviours for superior customer value",
  "Components", "Intelligence generation, dissemination, responsiveness", "Customer orientation, competitor orientation, interfunctional coordination",
  "Typical measure", "MARKOR (Kohli, Jaworski & Kumar, 1993)", "Narver & Slater multi-item scale",
  "Unit of focus", "Activities and processes", "Values, norms, and coordination",
  "Managerial lever", "Information systems, cross-functional routines, incentives", "Leadership, shared values, hiring and socialization"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Two conceptualizations of market orientation.")
```

### Core logic and propositions

The logic links information to action. Firms that know more about what customers
value, and about what competitors are about to offer, can design better
offerings and react faster. That knowledge has value only if it reaches the
people who design, price, and deliver the offering, and only if they act on it.
Hence the theory's central propositions:

- **P1 (Performance).** Market orientation is positively related to business
  performance [@narver1990; @jaworski1993].
- **P2 (Antecedents).** Top-management emphasis, interdepartmental connectedness,
  and market-based reward systems increase market orientation. Interdepartmental
  conflict and centralization reduce it [@jaworski1993].
- **P3 (Mediation).** The effect on performance runs largely through
  innovativeness, product and service quality, and customer loyalty
  [@kirca2005].
- **P4 (Environment).** Market orientation should matter more when customer
  preferences change quickly and competition is intense, although empirical
  support for this moderation is weak [@jaworski1993].
- **P5 (Employee outcomes).** Market orientation is associated with stronger
  employee commitment and esprit de corps [@jaworski1993].

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-ms-mo) summarizes this structure.

```{r fig-ms-mo, fig.cap = "Mechanism of market orientation. Organizational antecedents shape the generation, dissemination, and use of market intelligence. Market orientation improves performance mainly through innovativeness, quality, and customer loyalty. Environmental conditions and the type of business moderate the effect. Synthesised from Jaworski and Kohli (1993) and Kirca et al. (2005).", fig.height = 3.8}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  A [label = "Antecedents\\n(top-management emphasis,\\nconnectedness, reward systems)", %s]
  G [label = "Intelligence\\ngeneration", %s]
  D [label = "Intelligence\\ndissemination", %s]
  R [label = "Responsiveness", %s]
  M [label = "Innovativeness,\\nquality, loyalty", %s]
  P [label = "Business\\nperformance", %s]
  E [label = "Environment and\\nbusiness type", %s]
  A -> G
  G -> D -> R
  R -> M -> P
  E -> M [style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

### Evidence and extensions

Hundreds of studies have tested the market orientation-performance link across
industries and countries. The meta-analysis by @kirca2005 synthesised this
literature and found a positive relationship with overall business performance,
with innovativeness, customer loyalty, and quality acting as mediators. The
relationship was stronger in manufacturing than in service firms and in national
cultures with lower power distance and uncertainty avoidance, which links the
theory to research on [culture](#hofstede) (Section \@ref(hofstede)). Top-management emphasis,
interdepartmental connectedness, and market-based reward systems emerged as
reliable antecedents.

A second stream asks what kind of market orientation matters. @narver2004
distinguish **responsive** market orientation, which addresses customers'
expressed needs, from **proactive** market orientation, which tries to discover
latent needs that customers cannot yet articulate. In their data, the proactive
form was the stronger predictor of new-product success.

::: {.debate}
**Can listening to customers be dangerous?** Studies of disk-drive makers by
@christensen1996 showed that leading firms failed in part *because* they
listened carefully to their largest existing customers, who did not want the
smaller, lower-performing drives that later displaced them. Read narrowly, this
looks like a refutation of market orientation. Read carefully, it shows that the
theory's boundary conditions matter: a responsive orientation focused on current
mainstream customers can blind a firm to emerging segments and technologies
[@christensen1997]. The proactive extension [@narver2004] and the original
definition's emphasis on *future* needs [@kohli1990] partly address the critique.
Two methodological concerns remain. Most evidence relies on cross-sectional,
single-informant surveys in which managers rate both orientation and performance,
which inflates correlations through common-method variance. And because
successful firms can afford more market research, reverse causality is hard to
rule out.
:::

### Applications in business

Market orientation is a practical diagnostic. A business can audit each step in
the intelligence chain. Is customer information collected beyond satisfaction
surveys, including complaints, front-line observations, and lost-sale analysis?
Does it reach product, operations, and finance, or does it stay in the marketing
department? And is anyone accountable for acting on it within a defined time?

::: {.business-case}
**Market orientation in retailing.** Two well-documented retailers illustrate
different routes to the same capability. Tesco's Clubcard loyalty programme,
launched in the United Kingdom in the mid-1990s and analysed with the data
science firm dunnhumby (which Tesco later took over), turned transaction data
into intelligence used for ranging, promotions, and personalized offers. This is
a strong form of *intelligence generation and dissemination*. Inditex's Zara
built *responsiveness*: store managers report what customers ask for and what
sells, central design teams turn those signals into new items, and short
production cycles let the firm act on intelligence within weeks rather than
seasons. The lesson for managers is that data collection alone is not market
orientation. Clubcard data created value because it changed decisions, and
Zara's store reports mattered because the supply chain could respond to them.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Market orientation will be positively related to new-product
  performance, and this effect will be mediated by product innovativeness.
- *H2.* The positive effect of responsive market orientation on performance will
  be weaker, and the effect of proactive orientation stronger, in markets with
  high technological turbulence.
- *H3.* Market-based reward systems will strengthen the link between
  intelligence dissemination and responsiveness.

**Measures.** MARKOR [@kohli1993], the Narver and Slater scale [@narver1990],
responsive and proactive scales [@narver2004]. Objective performance from
financial databases rather than self-reports where possible.

**Designs.** Multi-informant surveys with lagged objective outcomes, panel
designs that track changes in orientation over time, and text analysis of annual
reports or earnings calls as an unobtrusive measure of customer focus.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Equating market orientation with "doing what customers say".** The construct
concerns the *process* of generating, sharing, and acting on intelligence about
current *and future* needs and about competitors. Measuring only customer
satisfaction or survey activity misses dissemination and responsiveness, and
treating stated preferences as the whole of market intelligence invites the
trap Christensen documented.
:::

## Service-Dominant Logic {#service-dominant-logic}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Service, the application of knowledge and skills for the benefit
of another party, is the fundamental basis of all exchange. Goods are vehicles
for service, and value is co-created by multiple actors and determined by the
beneficiary in use.

**Origins.** Marketing theory. @vargo2004, refined in @vargo2008 and @vargo2016,
building on services-marketing work such as @shostack1977.

**Level of analysis.** Market, service ecosystem, and actor-to-actor exchange.

**Key constructs.** Service (singular), operant and operand resources, value
co-creation, value-in-use, value proposition, resource integration, service
ecosystem, institutions.

**Boundary conditions.** A lens or meta-theory rather than a set of directly
testable hypotheses. Most useful where value depends heavily on how customers
use and combine resources.

**Related theories.** [Market orientation](#market-orientation),
[Resource-advantage theory](#resource-advantage-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-advantage-theory)),
[Social exchange theory](#social-exchange-theory) (Section \@ref(social-exchange-theory)),
[Commitment-trust theory](#commitment-trust-theory) (Section \@ref(commitment-trust-theory)),
[Institutional theory](#institutional-theory) (Section \@ref(institutional-theory)).
:::

### Origins and core logic

Marketing grew out of economics, and economics grew up studying the production
and exchange of tangible goods. Services were long treated as a residual
category, defined by what they lacked: they were *intangible*, *heterogeneous*,
*inseparable* from consumption, and *perishable*. @shostack1977 argued that
marketing needed to "break free" from product thinking, because most offerings
combine tangible and intangible elements.

@vargo2004 went further. They argued that the goods-services distinction itself
is the problem. In their **service-dominant (S-D) logic**, *service*, in the
singular, is the process of using one's competences for the benefit of another.
People exchange service for service, and goods are simply distribution
mechanisms for service: a car provides the service of transportation, and money
is a claim on future service. The theory distinguishes **operand resources**,
which must be acted on to be useful (raw materials, machines), from **operant
resources**, which act on other resources (knowledge, skills, relationships).
Operant resources, S-D logic argues, are the fundamental source of competitive
advantage, which connects the theory to the
[resource-based view](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)) and to
[resource-advantage theory](#resource-advantage-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-advantage-theory)) [@hunt1995].

The second core idea concerns value. Under **goods-dominant logic**, value is
created by the firm, embedded in the product, and realized at the point of sale
(**value-in-exchange**). Under S-D logic, value is realized when the beneficiary
integrates the offering with its own resources in a context of use
(**value-in-use**). The firm cannot deliver value on its own. It can only offer
**value propositions**, and the customer is always a co-creator of value
[@vargo2008]. The 2016 update consolidated the framework into five axioms and
added a fifth element: value co-creation is coordinated through actor-generated
**institutions** and institutional arrangements, such as norms, rules, and
shared meanings [@vargo2016].

::: {.definition}
**The five axioms of service-dominant logic** [@vargo2016]. (1) Service is the
fundamental basis of exchange. (2) Value is co-created by multiple actors,
always including the beneficiary. (3) All social and economic actors are
resource integrators. (4) Value is always uniquely and phenomenologically
determined by the beneficiary. (5) Value co-creation is coordinated through
actor-generated institutions and institutional arrangements.
:::

The axioms shift the unit of analysis away from the firm-customer dyad.
Because every actor integrates resources from many sources, a customer's
value-in-use depends on complementary offerings, other customers, and the rules
of the setting, not only on the focal firm. A smartphone delivers value through
apps, networks, and the user's own skills. A hospital stay delivers value
through clinicians, family members, and insurance arrangements. S-D logic calls
these nested systems **service ecosystems**, which links it to research on
[network effects](#network-effects) (Section \@ref(network-effects)) and [two-sided markets](#two-sided-markets) (Section \@ref(two-sided-markets)) (Table \@ref(tab:tab-ms-gdl-sdl)).

```{r tab-ms-gdl-sdl}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Dimension, ~`Goods-dominant logic`, ~`Service-dominant logic`,
  "Unit of exchange", "Goods (and services as a residual category)", "Service: applied knowledge and skills",
  "Role of goods", "End product that embodies value", "Vehicle or appliance for delivering service",
  "Primary resource", "Operand resources (materials, equipment)", "Operant resources (knowledge, skills, relationships)",
  "Locus of value", "Value-in-exchange, realized at sale", "Value-in-use, determined by the beneficiary",
  "Role of customer", "Target and recipient of value", "Co-creator and resource integrator",
  "Firm's role", "Produce and deliver value", "Offer value propositions and support co-creation",
  "Relationship focus", "Transactions", "Ongoing relationships within service ecosystems",
  "Business model example", "Selling an engine", "Charging per hour of engine availability"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Goods-dominant versus service-dominant logic, synthesised from Vargo and Lusch (2004, 2008, 2016).")
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-ms-sdl) represents value co-creation as resource
integration within an institutional context.

The customer integrates it with its own operant and operand resources in a context of use, and value-in-use is determined by the beneficiary. Institutions coordinate the process. Redrawn from the logic of Vargo and Lusch (2008, 2016).", fig.height = 3.6}

  F [label = "Firm resources\\n(knowledge, skills,\\nequipment)", %s]
  V [label = "Value\\nproposition", %s]
  C [label = "Customer resources\\n(skills, time, data,\\nother offerings)", %s]
